questions.title: Hierarchical Risk Parity vs. Mean-Variance Optimization
questions.prompt: A portfolio manager asks why you'd ever use Hierarchical Risk Parity instead of classical mean-variance optimization, given that mean-variance is theoretically optimal. Give your actual answer, including HRP's real tradeoff.
questions.modelAnswer: Mean-variance optimization is theoretically optimal only given a perfectly known covariance matrix and expected-return vector -- in practice, both are estimated with error, and mean-variance's optimal weights depend on inverting the covariance matrix, an operation that massively amplifies small estimation errors when assets are correlated, the normal case. The practical symptom is notorious: mean-variance portfolios frequently concentrate heavily in one or two assets whose estimated covariance happened to look slightly favorable, and those weights can flip wildly with a small change in the input data. HRP sidesteps the inversion entirely: it uses the correlation matrix's hierarchical clustering structure to recursively allocate weight between more-and-less-correlated groups, without ever needing Sigma^-1. The real tradeoff is that HRP gives up the theoretical optimality guarantee mean-variance has under perfect inputs -- it doesn't maximize any explicit expected-return/risk objective -- in exchange for weights that are demonstrably more stable and better-diversified out-of-sample when the inputs are noisy estimates rather than known quantities.
questions.professionalAnswer: My honest answer is that mean-variance's optimality is conditional on knowing the true covariance matrix and expected returns exactly, and we never actually know either -- we estimate them, with real error, and mean-variance's reliance on inverting the covariance matrix means that estimation error gets amplified, sometimes dramatically. What you get in practice is a portfolio that looks theoretically optimal on paper but concentrates in one or two names whose estimated covariance happened to look good that quarter, and can flip entirely with a small data revision. HRP never inverts anything -- it works off the correlation matrix's clustering structure directly. The real cost is that HRP doesn't actually maximize any explicit risk-adjusted return objective -- it's giving up that theoretical optimality on purpose, in exchange for weights that are a lot more stable and tend to hold up better out-of-sample, which in my experience matters more than theoretical optimality against inputs we can't estimate perfectly anyway.
questions.example: A simulation comparing Markowitz and HRP weights across repeated resamples of the same underlying data typically shows HRP's weights changing far less from resample to resample than Markowitz's, even though Markowitz would be optimal if the true covariance were known exactly.

Assuming HRP and mean-variance are solving the same problem, rather than trading optimality for stability

questions.prompt: Write the code to fit PCA on a standardized panel of daily returns for 200 stocks, extract the first three principal components, and explain what you'd expect the first component's loadings to look like if it's behaving as a genuine market factor.
questions.code:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

returns_std = scaler.fit_transform(returns.dropna())

If PC1 is behaving as a genuine market factor, its loadings should be roughly uniform in sign (nearly all positive, or nearly all negative, since PCA's sign is arbitrary) and of broadly comparable magnitude across most of the 200 stocks. A loading pattern that instead shows a cluster of large positive loadings and a cluster of large negative loadings would suggest PC1 is actually capturing something more like a sector or style spread rather than a pure market factor.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code itself is routine: standardize, fit PCA with n_components=3, and pull the loadings out of pca.components_. What I'd actually check first is explained_variance_ratio_ -- for a 200-stock panel, seeing the first component alone explain somewhere in the 30-50%+ range is the normal signature of a market factor, and a sharp drop-off after that tells me the remaining structure is much more modest. Then I'd look directly at the sign pattern of PC1's loadings: if it's genuinely a market factor, almost every stock should load with the same sign and roughly comparable size. If instead I see a clean split -- a cluster of large positive loadings and a cluster of large negative ones -- that's not a market factor at all, that's PC1 picking up something more like a sector or growth-versus-value spread, and I'd want to know that before treating PC1 as 'the market' in any downstream risk model.

questions.title: Tuning a Gradient Boosted Model Against Overfitting on Faint Signal
questions.prompt: Write the code to fit an XGBoost regressor on financial features with early stopping, and explain which specific hyperparameters you'd lean on hardest to prevent it from fitting noise, given that real signal here is often under 2% of variance.
questions.code:
from xgboost import XGBRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X_train, y_train, test_size=0.2, shuffle=False)

model = XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=1000, learning_rate=0.02, max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.7, colsample_bytree=0.7,
    reg_alpha=0.1, reg_lambda=1.0,
    early_stopping_rounds=50, eval_metric="rmse", random_state=0,
)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)
questions.modelAnswer: Early stopping is the first line of defense: it halts training once validation error stops improving, letting the data decide how many boosting rounds are actually useful rather than guessing n_estimators up front. Beyond that, the two knobs I'd lean on hardest for genuinely faint signal are max_depth and learning_rate: keeping max_depth shallow (2-3) limits how many high-order feature interactions each tree can fit, which matters because with 1-2% real signal, deep trees have ample room to carve out interactions that fit noise; a small learning_rate (0.01-0.03) forces the model to take many small steps rather than a few large, confident ones, making it harder for the ensemble to lock onto a noisy pattern early and run with it. subsample and colsample_bytree below 1.0 add further regularization, and reg_alpha/reg_lambda directly penalize large leaf weights, which otherwise concentrate when a few splits happen to fit noise well on the training set.
questions.professionalAnswer: The setup itself is the standard pattern: hold out a validation slice, set a generous n_estimators cap, and let early_stopping_rounds decide the real number of trees rather than guessing. But if I had to name the two levers I'd actually tune hardest given how faint real signal is here, it's max_depth and learning_rate. Shallow trees, depth 2 or 3, limit how much interaction complexity each tree can chase, which matters a lot when 98%+ of the variance is noise. A small learning_rate forces the ensemble to move in small, cautious steps instead of quickly locking onto whatever pattern the first few rounds happen to find, and paired with early stopping, that combination is what actually keeps the model honest. I'd also lean on subsample and colsample_bytree below 1 so no single tree ever sees the whole dataset or feature set at once, and reg_alpha/reg_lambda to keep leaf weights from blowing up around a handful of rows that happened to fit well by chance.

questions.title: Implementing Walk-Forward Validation and Explaining Its Limits
questions.prompt: Write the code to build an expanding-window walk-forward validation loop for a return-prediction model using TimeSeriesSplit, and explain the specific gap this still leaves open that the next validation technique in the curriculum has to close.
questions.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)
scores = []
for train_idx, test_idx in tscv.split(X):
    X_train, X_test = X.iloc[train_idx], X.iloc[test_idx]
    y_train, y_test = y.iloc[train_idx], y.iloc[test_idx]
    model = Ridge(alpha=5.0).fit(X_train, y_train)

This is a genuine improvement, but it isn't sufficient on its own when labels are forward-looking: if the label is a 5-day-forward return, a training observation sitting just before the test boundary still has a label window that reaches a few days into the test period, even though the observation's own timestamp is safely in the training window. TimeSeriesSplit has no concept of label windows -- it only looks at row position -- so this leak survives walk-forward validation entirely. The next technique, purging (and embargoing), closes exactly this gap by filtering training rows based on where their label actually resolves relative to the test span, not merely where the row itself sits in time.
questions.professionalAnswer: The loop itself is the standard TimeSeriesSplit pattern: each fold's test set comes strictly after its training set in calendar order, which already fixes the big problem with plain KFold, where most folds end up training on data from after the test period. But I'd flag immediately that this isn't the end of the story for financial labels specifically. If the label is a forward-looking return -- say 5 days ahead -- a training row sitting right before the test boundary still has a label that reaches a few days into the test period, even though its own timestamp is cleanly in the training window. TimeSeriesSplit has no idea about that, because it only ever looks at row position, never at where a label's window actually ends. That's precisely the leak purging exists to close.

questions.title: Fitting ARIMA and Choosing the Differencing Order Honestly
questions.prompt: Write the code to fit an ARIMA model to a non-stationary log-price series in statsmodels, and explain how you'd actually decide the differencing order d rather than just guessing d=1.
questions.code:
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

d = 0
series = log_prices.copy()
while adfuller(series.dropna())[1] > 0.05 and d < 2:
    series = series.diff()
    d += 1

forecast = fit.get_forecast(steps=10)
questions.modelAnswer: The differencing order d should be chosen by actually testing for stationarity at each level, not assumed as d=1 by convention. The practical procedure: run the ADF test on the raw series; if it fails to reject the unit-root null, difference once and re-test; if the once-differenced series rejects the null, d=1 is confirmed; if it still doesn't reject, difference again, capping at d=2 in practice since over-differencing introduces its own artifacts -- notably a strong, spurious negative MA(1) signature. Blindly setting d=1 for log prices is usually right in practice, but 'usually right' and 'verified' are different things, and a series with a structural break or unusually strong momentum can behave differently -- checking with the ADF test at each step is cheap insurance against quietly over- or under-differencing.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code itself fits the model once d is decided, but the part I'd actually be careful about is not just defaulting to d=1 out of habit. My real process is to run the ADF test on the raw log-price series first; if it fails to reject the unit-root null, I difference once and re-test, and if that differenced series now rejects the null, d=1 is confirmed by the data, not just assumed. If it still doesn't reject after one difference, I'll difference again, but I cap that at d=2 in practice, because over-differencing isn't harmless -- it introduces a strong, spurious negative MA(1) pattern that can look like real structure in the ACF if you're not watching for it. d=1 is the right answer for most log-price series, which is exactly why it's such a common default, but I'd rather confirm that with an actual ADF test than assume it blindly.

import pandas as pd

A significant result establishes exactly one thing: past values of series A contain information that improves the statistical prediction of series B, beyond what B's own history already provides. It does not establish that A physically or economically causes B -- two series can show Granger causality purely because both respond, with different lags, to a common third driver that isn't in the model at all, exactly analogous to an omitted-variable problem in ordinary regression. It also says nothing about the sign, size, or stability of the relationship over time.

The part I'd be careful to spell out is what a significant result here actually means, because the name is genuinely misleading. All it tells you is that past values of one series add statistically useful information for predicting the other, on top of that series' own history -- it is explicitly not a claim about real causation. I'd watch for the classic trap: two series can both be driven by some third factor not in the model, each with a slightly different lag, and that alone can produce a 'Granger causes' result between them with no real causal link at all. I'd also point out that a significant result says nothing about how strong or stable the relationship is over time.

questions.title: Implementing Fama-MacBeth to Estimate a Risk Premium
questions.prompt: Write the code to implement a simplified Fama-MacBeth two-step regression estimating a factor's risk premium, and explain exactly why its standard error formula is different from -- and more honest than -- a naive single cross-sectional regression's.
questions.code:
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm

lambdas = []
for t in dates:
    y_t = returns.loc[t]
    X_t = sm.add_constant(betas)
    res_t = sm.OLS(y_t, X_t).fit()
    lambdas.append(res_t.params["beta"])

lambdas = pd.Series(lambdas, index=dates)

questions.modelAnswer: Step 1 estimates each asset's beta once from a time-series regression. Step 2 runs a fresh cross-sectional regression of returns on those betas at every single time period t, producing a time series of period-specific risk-premium estimates lambda_t rather than one number. The final estimate is the average of that series, and its standard error is computed from the standard deviation of the lambda_t series itself, divided by sqrt(T) -- treating each period's cross-sectional estimate as one observation of an underlying random variable. A naive single cross-sectional regression reports a standard error from that single regression's residual variance, which doesn't account for the fact that the betas on the right-hand side are themselves noisy estimates -- the errors-in-variables problem. Fama-MacBeth's period-to-period variability in lambda_t implicitly captures exactly this additional source of uncertainty, which is why its standard error is typically larger, and more honest, than the naive single-regression number.
questions.professionalAnswer: The code has two distinct stages: betas get estimated once per asset from a time-series regression, and then a brand new cross-sectional regression gets run separately at every single period, generating a whole series of lambda_t estimates rather than one number. The final risk premium is just the average of that series, but the standard error is where Fama-MacBeth earns its reputation -- it's the standard deviation of the lambda_t series itself, divided by the square root of the number of periods. A single naive cross-sectional regression doesn't do that -- it reports a standard error from one regression's residuals, which quietly assumes the betas on the right-hand side are the true values, when really they're themselves estimated with error. That errors-in-variables problem is exactly what makes the naive single-regression standard error too optimistic.
questions.example: On real equity data, a Fama-MacBeth standard error for a factor's risk premium is often visibly larger than the standard error from a single naive cross-sectional regression on the same betas -- a direct sign that the naive approach was overstating confidence.
commonMistakes: Running only one cross-sectional regression instead of one per time period
Computing the standard error from a single regression's residuals rather than from the cross-period variability of lambda_t
Not recognizing the errors-in-variables problem that makes the naive single-regression standard error overconfident
Forgetting that betas are estimated once (time-series step) but lambda_t is re-estimated every period (cross-sectional step)
keyPoints: Fama-MacBeth runs one cross-sectional regression per time period, not just once
The final estimate is the time-series average of lambda_t; the standard error is std(lambda_t)/sqrt(T)
A naive single cross-sectional regression's standard error doesn't account for estimation error in the betas themselves
Fama-MacBeth's period-to-period variability honestly captures that extra uncertainty, giving a more defensible standard error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct two-step Fama-MacBeth implementation
Correctly explains the standard-error construction via cross-period variability
Correctly explains the errors-in-variables problem with the naive alternative

questions.title: Solve, Don't Invert: A NumPy Habit That Actually Matters
questions.prompt: Write the code to solve for a minimum-variance portfolio's unnormalized weights using both np.linalg.solve and np.linalg.inv, and explain concretely why a quant research team would enforce the first as a code-review standard.
questions.code:
import numpy as np

Sigma = np.array([[0.04, 0.01], [0.01, 0.09]])
ones = np.ones(2)

w_unnorm_solve = np.linalg.solve(Sigma, ones)

w_unnorm_inv = np.linalg.inv(Sigma) @ ones
questions.modelAnswer: Both lines compute the same mathematical quantity, Sigma^-1 @ ones, and on a small, well-conditioned matrix they'll even return numerically identical results. The reason a code-review standard would still enforce solve over inv is that np.linalg.inv explicitly computes the full inverse matrix as an intermediate step, which is both more computationally expensive and less numerically stable than directly solving the linear system, especially as the covariance matrix grows larger or becomes closer to singular. np.linalg.solve uses a more numerically robust factorization-based approach (effectively LU decomposition) that avoids ever forming the explicit inverse. Enforcing solve as a standard isn't pedantry over a toy case; it's defending against the much larger, worse-conditioned matrices the same code will eventually be run on in production.
questions.professionalAnswer: Both versions compute the exact same thing mathematically, and on a tiny, well-behaved matrix they'll agree to many decimal places -- so at first glance the review comment can look like pedantry. The actual reason I'd still flag inv in review is that it explicitly builds the full inverse matrix as an intermediate step, which costs roughly three times the floating-point work of solve and, more importantly, is less numerically stable once the matrix gets larger or starts approaching singular, which is exactly the territory a real covariance matrix with hundreds of correlated assets lives in. solve uses a more robust factorization approach under the hood and never actually forms that explicit inverse. The toy example in a code review doesn't show the difference, which is precisely why I'd still insist on the habit -- the same function gets reused later on matrices where the difference is no longer cosmetic.
questions.example: On a well-conditioned small matrix, solve and inv agree to machine precision; on a large, near-singular covariance matrix, inv's extra computational path can introduce materially more numerical error than solve's direct factorization approach.
commonMistakes: Treating np.linalg.inv and np.linalg.solve as interchangeable because they agree on small, well-conditioned examples
Not recognizing that inv explicitly forms the full inverse as an unnecessary, costlier intermediate step
Assuming numerical stability only matters for 'big' or exotic problems rather than routine production risk code
Enforcing a coding standard without being able to explain the concrete numerical-stability reason behind it
keyPoints: np.linalg.solve and np.linalg.inv @ b compute the same mathematical result
inv explicitly forms the full inverse matrix, costing more computation and more accumulated numerical error
solve uses a more numerically robust, factorization-based approach that avoids forming the explicit inverse
The difference matters most on large or poorly conditioned matrices, exactly the regime of real risk models

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct code demonstrating both approaches
Correctly explains the numerical-stability and performance difference
Connects the difference to why it matters in a real production risk-model context

questions.title: Your R-Squared of 8% Is a Red Flag, Not a Win
questions.prompt: A junior teammate is excited that their new return-prediction model posted an out-of-sample R-squared of 8%, well above the 1-2% they were told to expect. How do you respond, and what's your actual investigation plan?
questions.modelAnswer: An out-of-sample R-squared of 8% on a return-prediction task is not good news on its own -- financial markets are close enough to efficient that an R-squared above roughly 5% should immediately raise suspicion of leakage rather than celebration of skill, precisely because genuinely exploitable, easily-found patterns of that strength would already be competed away. My investigation plan would start with the most common and most damaging culprit: check every feature for whether it could have used information not actually available at the time of prediction -- a rolling window that includes the current or a future bar, a fundamental field using a restated rather than originally-reported value, or a target leaking into a feature through a shared calculation. Next, check the cross-validation setup itself for the classic walk-forward-without-purging leak, where training labels with forward-looking windows overlap the test period. Finally, check whether the universe or feature set changed between training and test in a way that introduces survivorship bias. An 8% out-of-sample R-squared on real financial data is far more often a bug than a breakthrough.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be honest with them immediately rather than letting the excitement run: an 8% out-of-sample R-squared on return prediction is not a result I'd celebrate without investigating first, because real, exploitable signal in markets this efficient almost never gets anywhere near that strong -- 1-2% is strong, and anything comfortably above 5% should trigger suspicion before congratulations. My actual plan is to walk through the usual leakage suspects in order of how often I've actually seen them cause this: first, every feature, checking specifically whether any rolling window includes the current or a future bar, or uses a fundamental value that was restated after the fact; second, the validation split itself, checking whether labels with forward-looking windows are leaking across the train/test boundary without purging; third, whether the universe itself changed between train and test in a way that quietly introduces survivorship bias. I'd frame this to the teammate not as 'you made a mistake' but as 'this is exactly the number that should make all of us go check for a bug.'
questions.example: A 'too good' out-of-sample R-squared is frequently traced to one specific line: a feature computed with .rolling(20).mean() applied to a column that wasn't shifted, so the window silently includes the current row's own target-adjacent value.
commonMistakes: Celebrating an unusually strong out-of-sample result instead of treating it as the first sign of a possible bug
Not having a concrete, ordered investigation plan for the most common leakage culprits
Checking only the feature code and skipping the validation/cross-validation setup itself
Assuming a strong result that 'passed' cross-validation is automatically free of leakage
keyPoints: In efficient markets, an unusually high out-of-sample R-squared for return prediction should trigger suspicion, not celebration
The most common culprit is a feature using information not actually available at prediction time
The validation setup itself (unpurged overlapping labels) is a second common leakage source
Universe changes between train and test periods are a third, less obvious source of distortion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds with appropriate skepticism rather than celebration, with correct reasoning
Proposes a concrete, ordered investigation plan covering the main leakage culprits
Handles the junior teammate's reaction constructively

questions.title: A Triple-Barrier Label Set Is Producing Suspiciously Clean Classes
questions.prompt: You switch a model from fixed-horizon labeling to the triple-barrier method, and the resulting labels look suspiciously clean -- almost no neutral (time-barrier) outcomes, nearly everything resolves to a clear win or loss. What would you check, and what's the most likely cause?
questions.modelAnswer: The triple-barrier method assigns a label based on which of three barriers is touched first, and the most likely cause of almost no time-barrier outcomes is that the profit-take and stop-loss barriers are set too tight relative to the asset's actual volatility and the chosen max holding period, so nearly every path touches a price barrier well before the time barrier ever gets a chance to matter. The check: compare the barrier width against the asset's realized volatility over the holding horizon -- if barriers are set at 0.5% while the asset's typical move over the holding period is 2-3%, almost every path resolves on a price barrier almost immediately. A second thing worth checking is whether the barriers are a fixed absolute return rather than scaled by each asset's own recent volatility -- a fixed barrier applied across assets or periods with very different volatility produces exactly this kind of systematically skewed label distribution.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first guess here is that the profit-take and stop-loss barriers are just set too tight relative to how much the asset actually moves over the holding period -- if the barriers are a fraction of the asset's typical volatility over that horizon, almost every path is going to touch one of them well before the time barrier ever triggers. The check I'd run first is comparing the barrier width directly against realized volatility over the holding window. I'd also check whether the barriers are a single global number applied to every asset, rather than scaled by each asset's own recent volatility, because that's a very common way to get this exact bug when labeling a cross-section of assets with different volatility profiles.
questions.example: Setting profit-take and stop-loss barriers at a fixed 2x the recent 20-day volatility, rather than a single global return threshold, typically restores a healthy mix of win/loss/neutral outcomes across assets with different volatility profiles.
commonMistakes: Setting profit-take/stop-loss barriers as a fixed global return rather than scaled by each asset's own volatility
Not comparing barrier width against realized volatility over the chosen holding horizon before trusting the label distribution
Assuming a 'cleaner-looking' label distribution is automatically a sign the labeling method is working better
Not checking whether the max holding period itself is set unreasonably long relative to the barrier widths
keyPoints: Triple-barrier labels resolve on whichever of profit-take, stop-loss, or max-time triggers first
Barriers set too tight relative to the asset's realized volatility cause almost all paths to resolve on a price barrier quickly
Fixed, non-volatility-scaled barriers applied across assets with different volatility profiles produce a skewed label distribution
A healthy label distribution usually requires barriers scaled to each asset's own recent volatility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies barrier width vs. volatility mismatch as the likely cause
Proposes a concrete diagnostic check (comparing barrier width to realized volatility)
Proposes the volatility-scaled barrier fix

questions.title: A Backtest That's Too Good Because of Who's in the Universe
questions.prompt: A backtest on 'S&P 500 stocks since 2005' shows a surprisingly strong and consistent long-only strategy with almost no large drawdowns relative to the index. What specific data construction mistake would you check for first, and how would you verify it?
questions.modelAnswer: The first and most likely culprit is survivorship bias in how the universe was constructed: if 'S&P 500 stocks since 2005' was built from today's current constituent list projected backward, every company removed from the index for underperformance, bankruptcy, or acquisition-at-a-discount since 2005 is silently excluded, and the surviving set is systematically tilted toward winners by construction -- producing exactly the pattern described. The verification is concrete: check whether the universe list used in the backtest changes over time (point-in-time membership) or is static across the whole sample; if it's static and matches today's constituents, that's the smoking gun. A proper fix requires a survivorship-bias-free, point-in-time index membership history, including delisted and removed names with their actual historical returns up to removal.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first suspicion is survivorship bias baked into how the universe itself was built -- if 'S&P 500 since 2005' actually means today's 500 constituents with their full history pulled backward, then every name that got removed for underperforming, going bankrupt, or getting acquired below its former price has been quietly dropped from the entire sample, and what's left is systematically tilted toward the names that happened to survive and do well. The way I'd verify it is simple: check whether the universe list is static across the whole backtest period and matches today's constituents, or whether it actually changes over time to reflect real historical membership. If it's static, that confirms it, and the fix is to source a genuine point-in-time, survivorship-bias-free constituent history instead.
questions.example: A backtest run on today's static S&P 500 list projected back to 2005 would have silently excluded names like Lehman Brothers and Washington Mutual -- each one a real historical loss an investor following the actual index would have had to live through.
commonMistakes: Not checking whether the backtest's universe reflects today's constituents or true historical, point-in-time membership
Assuming a smooth, strong backtest result is evidence of strategy skill before checking the universe construction
Treating 'S&P 500 since 2005' as self-evidently meaning the real historical index, without verifying the data source
Not sourcing a proper survivorship-bias-free constituent history as the actual fix
keyPoints: A static, today's-constituents universe applied backward silently excludes every historically removed name
That exclusion systematically tilts the backtest toward surviving winners, inflating apparent performance
The diagnostic check is whether the universe list changes over time to reflect true historical membership
The fix is a genuine point-in-time, survivorship-bias-free constituent history

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies survivorship bias as the likely cause
Proposes a concrete, correct verification check
Proposes the correct fix (point-in-time constituent data)

questions.title: Your OLS Standard Errors Are Lying to You
questions.prompt: You regress a strategy's daily returns on a set of factor exposures and get a strong, significant alpha with default OLS standard errors. A colleague points out the regression residuals show clear autocorrelation. What exactly goes wrong here, and what do you check next?
questions.modelAnswer: Autocorrelated residuals violate the no-autocorrelation Gauss-Markov assumption, and while this doesn't bias the OLS point estimate of alpha itself, it does invalidate the default standard-error formula, which assumes independent errors. Positive autocorrelation (the common case for daily financial residuals) causes the default OLS standard error to be understated, making alpha look more statistically significant than it actually is. The check I'd run next is a Ljung-Box test or visual inspection of the residual ACF to confirm and quantify the autocorrelation, then re-run the significance test using Newey-West (HAC) standard errors. If alpha's significance survives the switch to Newey-West standard errors, that's a real result; if not, the original 'significant alpha' was substantially an artifact of the wrong standard-error formula.
questions.professionalAnswer: The autocorrelation itself doesn't bias alpha -- the point estimate survives fine -- but it does break the formula OLS uses to compute standard errors, which assumes the residuals are independent. Daily financial residuals are commonly positively autocorrelated, and positive autocorrelation specifically makes the default standard error too small, which means the t-stat on alpha looks more impressive than it should. What I'd check next is straightforward: run a Ljung-Box test on the residuals to confirm and quantify the autocorrelation, then redo the significance test with Newey-West standard errors. If alpha stays significant after that correction, I'd trust the result. If not, that tells me the original 'significant alpha' was mostly an artifact of using a standard-error formula that assumed something the data clearly doesn't satisfy.
questions.example: A strategy's alpha t-stat might drop from 3.1 under default OLS standard errors to 1.4 under Newey-West correction with a handful of lags -- the same point estimate, a very different conclusion about statistical significance.
commonMistakes: Believing autocorrelated residuals bias the alpha estimate itself, rather than just its standard error
Not checking the direction of the bias: positive autocorrelation typically understates the standard error, not overstates it
Reporting the default OLS t-stat as final without testing and correcting for residual autocorrelation
Not using a formal test (Ljung-Box) to confirm autocorrelation rather than relying on visual impression alone
keyPoints: Autocorrelated residuals don't bias OLS's point estimate, but they do invalidate the default standard-error formula
Positive autocorrelation (common in financial residuals) typically understates the default standard error
Ljung-Box tests and residual ACF plots confirm and quantify the autocorrelation
Newey-West (HAC) standard errors correct for both autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity in the significance test

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes bias in alpha from the standard-error problem
Correctly identifies the direction of the standard-error distortion
Proposes the correct diagnostic (Ljung-Box) and fix (Newey-West)

questions.title: A Technical-Indicator Feature Set Looks Great In-Sample and Means Nothing
questions.prompt: A junior researcher built a model on 40 technical indicators (various SMAs, EMAs, RSI windows, MACD variants) and reports strong in-sample feature importance scores for several of them. Why should you be skeptical before even looking at out-of-sample performance?
questions.modelAnswer: Every one of those 40 indicators is built from nothing but the price series itself, run through a smoothing or rescaling transform -- SMAs and EMAs are low-pass filters of price, RSI is a bounded transform of recent momentum, MACD is the difference of two smooths of price -- which means the whole feature set is highly collinear with each other and with simple lagged returns. In that setting, in-sample feature-importance scores are close to meaningless: with many near-duplicate, highly-correlated features, a tree or linear model can distribute importance somewhat arbitrarily among whichever of the 40 happened to split slightly more favorably on this specific training sample, partly reflecting which parameter variant was tried rather than independent predictive value. Before trusting any importance ranking, I'd check the feature set's own correlation structure directly -- a correlation matrix across all 40 would very likely reveal most of them cluster into a small handful of genuinely distinct signals.
questions.professionalAnswer: Before I even look at out-of-sample numbers, I'd be skeptical of the in-sample importance scores themselves, because every one of these 40 indicators is derived from nothing but the price series run through some smoothing or rescaling -- SMAs and EMAs are just low-pass filters on price, RSI is a bounded transform of recent momentum, MACD is a difference of two smooths of the same thing. That means this isn't really 40 independent features, it's a handful of genuinely distinct signals wearing 40 different costumes, and that heavy collinearity is exactly what makes in-sample feature importance unreliable -- a tree model splitting on whichever of several near-duplicate indicators happened to look slightly better on this particular training sample isn't finding real signal. I'd want to see a correlation matrix across all 40 features before trusting any individual importance ranking, because I'd bet most of them cluster into just a few actually distinct signals.
questions.example: A correlation matrix across SMA(10), SMA(20), EMA(12), EMA(26) typically shows pairwise correlations above 0.9 -- these are nominally four different features that are carrying almost the same single piece of information.
commonMistakes: Trusting in-sample feature importance on a highly collinear feature set as if each feature were independent
Not checking the correlation structure across the feature set before interpreting any individual importance score
Treating 40 differently-named technical indicators as 40 independent sources of information
Not accounting for how many parameter variants were likely tried, inflating the appearance of a strong in-sample result
keyPoints: Technical indicators are transformations or smooths of price, carrying highly overlapping information
In-sample feature importance on collinear features is distributed partly arbitrarily, not purely by genuine signal
Checking a correlation matrix (or VIF) across the feature set reveals how few genuinely distinct signals exist
Many tried parameter variants (window lengths, smoothing constants) further inflate apparent in-sample strength

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why technical indicators are highly collinear by construction
Correctly explains why in-sample importance is unreliable under heavy collinearity
Proposes a concrete check (correlation matrix/VIF) before trusting the result
Clarity

questions.title: A Global Z-Score Is Quietly Leaking the Future
questions.prompt: You find that a feature in your pipeline is normalized using (x - x.mean()) / x.std() computed once over the entire dataset, training and test combined. Explain precisely what's wrong with this, including a subtlety beyond the obvious leakage.
questions.modelAnswer: Computing the mean and standard deviation once over the entire dataset, including the test period, means every training observation's normalized value was computed using statistics that incorporate future information relative to that observation's own timestamp -- a textbook leakage pattern. The less obvious subtlety is that even setting leakage aside, a single global z-score assumes the feature's distribution is stable across the entire sample, which is rarely true for financial features -- a regime change partway through the sample changes the feature's true mean and variance, and a single global normalization silently blends pre- and post-regime statistics into one number that doesn't correctly represent either period. The fix for both problems at once is a rolling z-score: subtract a rolling mean and divide by a rolling standard deviation computed only from a trailing window, which uses only information available at that point and adapts to a drifting mean or changing volatility regime.
questions.professionalAnswer: The leakage itself is the obvious part: a mean and standard deviation computed over the whole dataset, test period included, means every training row's normalized value secretly incorporates information from after that row's own timestamp. But there's a second problem that's easy to miss even if you fixed the leakage by using only the training set's mean and std: a single global z-score assumes the feature's distribution doesn't change across the whole sample, and that's rarely true for financial data -- a volatility regime shift partway through the sample means the feature's real mean and variance are genuinely different before and after, and one frozen global number blends those two different realities into something that doesn't correctly describe either one. The fix that solves both problems at once is a rolling z-score, computed from a trailing window at each point in time.
questions.example: A feature normalized with a global z-score computed over 2015-2024 would silently use 2023-2024's volatility regime to normalize a 2016 observation, distorting both the leakage picture and the feature's true historical behavior.
commonMistakes: Computing normalization statistics (mean, std) over the full dataset including the test period
Fixing only the leakage (using train-only statistics) while still assuming the feature's distribution is stable across time
Not recognizing that a regime change partway through the sample breaks a single global normalization
Not using a rolling, trailing-window normalization that adapts to a drifting mean or variance
keyPoints: A global z-score computed over the full dataset leaks future information into every training observation's normalized value
Even a train-only global z-score still assumes the feature's distribution is stable across the whole sample
A regime change partway through the sample breaks that stability assumption, blending two different realities into one number
A rolling z-score (trailing window) fixes both the leakage and the stability assumption simultaneously

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the leakage problem with a global, full-dataset z-score
Correctly identifies the additional, less obvious distributional-stability problem
Proposes the rolling z-score as the fix for both issues

questions.title: 1,000 Strategies, Some Will Look Great by Chance Alone
questions.prompt: Your team's research pipeline has tested roughly 1,000 parameter variations of a strategy family over the past year, and the best one has a backtested Sharpe of 1.9. A risk officer asks you to justify why this isn't just the multiple-testing trap. What's your honest answer?
questions.modelAnswer: The honest starting point is to acknowledge the risk officer's instinct is exactly correct to raise: with 1,000 trials, even if every single variation had genuinely zero skill, basic probability guarantees some will show an impressively high historical Sharpe ratio purely by chance -- simulating 1,000 pure-noise strategies routinely produces a handful clearing a Sharpe of 1.5-2.0 with no real edge. The honest justification has to go beyond the single headline number: benchmark the 1.9 against the expected maximum Sharpe ratio from 1,000 zero-skill trials specifically (via a Deflated Sharpe Ratio calculation), check whether the 1,000 trials were genuinely independent or narrowed by economic reasoning at each step, and check performance on a genuinely untouched holdout period. If the strategy survives all three checks, there's a real case; if any is weak, the honest answer is that the 1.9 likely doesn't reflect real skill.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by telling the risk officer they're right to ask, because with 1,000 trials, pure chance alone guarantees some of them will post an impressive Sharpe ratio even with zero real skill behind any of them. So 1.9 as the best of 1,000, on its own, isn't distinguishable from what noise alone would produce. My actual justification would have three parts: first, I'd compute a Deflated Sharpe Ratio, which benchmarks the 1.9 against the expected maximum Sharpe from 1,000 zero-skill trials, not against zero. Second, I'd check how genuinely independent those 1,000 trials actually were. Third, and most importantly, I'd want performance on a holdout period that had zero influence on picking the winner. If all three hold up, I have a real case. If any one is weak, I'd tell the risk officer honestly that the 1.9 probably doesn't reflect real skill.
questions.example: A simulation of 1,000 pure-noise strategies at zero real skill routinely produces a maximum Sharpe ratio in the 1.5-2.0 range purely from the mechanics of taking a maximum over many trials -- a direct, numerical demonstration of exactly the risk the officer is flagging.
commonMistakes: Defending the 1.9 Sharpe by comparing it against zero instead of against the expected maximum under pure luck
Treating the raw count of 1,000 trials as the true number of independent tests without checking for structural overlap
Not having a genuinely untouched holdout period that played no role in selecting the winning configuration
Responding defensively to the risk officer instead of acknowledging the question is legitimate and well-founded
keyPoints: With 1,000 trials, pure chance alone produces some impressively high Sharpe ratios even with zero real skill
The Deflated Sharpe Ratio benchmarks the candidate against the expected maximum under that many trials, not against zero
The effective number of independent trials may be smaller than 1,000 if many variations share structure
A genuinely untouched holdout period, uninvolved in the original selection, is the strongest remaining evidence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Acknowledges the risk officer's concern as legitimate rather than defensive
Proposes the Deflated Sharpe Ratio as the correct quantitative benchmark
Addresses effective independence of trials and the need for a genuine holdout

questions.title: Designing a Research Data Layer That Won't Rot
questions.prompt: You're setting up a research data layer for a small team so that load_prices(universe, start, end) becomes the only way anyone touches market data. What does the interface need to guarantee, and what's the first thing that breaks if you skip the caching layer?
questions.modelAnswer: The core guarantee a research data layer has to provide is a stable output contract -- consistent column names, dtypes, and timezone handling -- so that research code written against load_prices never needs to know or care whether the underlying source is a CSV, a Parquet file, a REST API, or a database table; the source can change entirely without touching a single line of code built on top of it. Skipping the caching layer doesn't break correctness directly, but it breaks the practical usability of the abstraction: every call for the same (universe, start, end) combination re-reads or re-fetches the raw source from scratch, turning what should be a cheap, instant function call into a slow bottleneck -- friction that quietly pushes researchers back toward hardcoding their own direct file reads, exactly the fragmentation the data layer exists to prevent. A simple functools.lru_cache is often sufficient for a single research session; the deeper point is caching isn't a performance nice-to-have, it's what keeps the abstraction from being actively worse than the ad hoc approach it replaced.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd insist the interface guarantees is a stable contract -- consistent column names, dtypes, timezone handling -- every single time, regardless of what's actually behind it. That's the whole point: research code calls load_prices by meaning, never by file path, and the source underneath can change without anyone downstream needing to touch their code, as long as that contract never shifts. If I skip caching, the problem isn't correctness, it's that the abstraction stops being worth using -- every repeated call for the same universe and date range re-reads the raw source from scratch, and that friction is exactly what pushes people back toward their own ad hoc direct reads 'just this once,' which defeats the entire purpose of building the layer. Even something as simple as an lru_cache decorator is usually enough to keep the abstraction fast enough that nobody has a reason to bypass it.
questions.example: @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=32) on load_prices(universe, start, end) turns repeated calls with the same arguments within a session into free lookups rather than redundant file reads or API calls.

Treating caching as an optional performance optimization rather than what keeps the abstraction usable at all
Allowing the output contract (column names, dtypes, timezones) to vary depending on the underlying source
Not anticipating that slow repeated calls will push researchers back toward direct, ad hoc file reads
keyPoints: The interface's core guarantee is a stable output contract, independent of the underlying data source
Research code calls by meaning (load_prices(universe, start, end)), never by file path
Skipping caching doesn't break correctness, but makes the abstraction slow enough that people bypass it
A simple in-memory cache (e.g. lru_cache) is often sufficient to keep the layer fast within a research session

Correctly explains the practical consequence of skipping caching

questions.title: Designing Experiment Tracking So 'Reproduce Last Week's Result' Isn't Archaeology
questions.prompt: A teammate says 'I changed nothing in the code, but I can't reproduce last week's backtest number.' Design the experiment-tracking and data-versioning setup that would have prevented this from ever becoming a mystery.
questions.modelAnswer: A backtest result depends on three things -- code, parameters, and data -- and version control already handles code well, which is exactly why 'I changed nothing in the code' feels so confusing: it's true, and also not the whole story. The setup that prevents this requires two connected pieces. First, experiment tracking: every run logs its input parameters, resulting metrics, and output artifacts, timestamped and queryable later, so 'what parameters produced last week's number' is a lookup. Second, data versioning: computing and logging a content hash (SHA-256) of the exact data file used in each run, so 'was the data actually the same' is answerable with a direct comparison; for teams where data changes often, pinning dated snapshots keeps last week's exact input sitting on disk rather than silently replaced. With both in place, 'I can't reproduce this' becomes a five-minute lookup instead of an open-ended investigation.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the single most common 'mystery' failure mode in research, and it's almost never actually a mystery once you have the right two things logged. A result depends on code, parameters, and data -- git handles code, so 'I changed nothing in the code' can be entirely true and still not explain anything. What I'd set up is experiment tracking for every run -- parameters, metrics, and artifacts, logged with a timestamp -- so 'what exactly produced last week's number' becomes a lookup. And alongside that, data versioning at minimum means hashing the exact data file used in each run and logging that hash next to the run record. With both in place, the teammate's situation stops being a mystery -- they'd just pull up last week's run record, compare the logged data hash to today's file, and immediately see that a vendor restated a few values and the file's hash no longer matches.
questions.example: A run record logging {params: {...}, metrics: {sharpe: 1.34}, data_hash: 'a1b2c3...'} lets a researcher confirm in seconds whether today's data file hashes identically to what produced last week's result.
commonMistakes: Relying on git alone, assuming code version control is sufficient for full reproducibility
Not logging a data fingerprint (hash) alongside parameters and metrics for every run
Treating experiment tracking as optional overhead rather than the thing that turns archaeology into a lookup
Overwriting data files in place rather than keeping dated, versioned snapshots when data is pinned rather than hashed
keyPoints: A result depends on code, parameters, and data; git only covers code
Experiment tracking logs parameters, metrics, and artifacts per run, making 'what produced this result' a lookup
Data versioning (at minimum, hashing the exact file used) answers 'was the data the same' directly
Together, these turn 'I can't reproduce this' into a quick comparison rather than an open-ended investigation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies that code, parameters, and data are three separate reproducibility risks
Proposes a concrete experiment-tracking design
Proposes a concrete data-versioning/fingerprinting design
Clarity

questions.title: Graduating a Signal from Notebook to Tested Module
questions.prompt: A promising signal has been living entirely inside one researcher's Jupyter notebook for three months, with cells that no longer run top-to-bottom reliably. Design the process for graduating it into tested, shareable code, and explain the specific notebook failure mode that makes this urgent.
questions.modelAnswer: The urgent failure mode is the hidden-state trap: a notebook's visible cell order and its actual execution order are two different things, and only the kernel's live memory remembers the second one -- a variable defined in a cell that was later edited, reordered, or deleted can still be sitting in memory, making the notebook appear to work in the current session while being unable to reproduce the same result if run fresh, top to bottom. The single most important diagnostic before trusting anything further is Kernel -> Restart & Run All. The graduation process: confirm the notebook survives a clean restart-and-run-all; pull the core signal logic into a plain Python module with explicit function signatures and no hidden reliance on notebook-global state; write tests against that module; keep a thin notebook that imports and calls the tested module for exploration, rather than containing the logic itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd flag as genuinely urgent here is the hidden-state trap -- three months of editing cells in place is exactly how a notebook accumulates variables still sitting in memory from a since-deleted or since-reordered cell, so it looks like it works every time, but that's an illusion created by the live kernel's memory, not a property of the actual code on disk. The single most important thing to do before anything else is Kernel, Restart & Run All, top to bottom -- if that doesn't reproduce the reported result, the notebook has been lying about its own correctness. My graduation process from there: confirm it survives that clean restart first; pull just the core signal logic into a real Python module with explicit function arguments; write tests against that module; and keep a much thinner notebook that imports and calls the tested module, rather than containing the actual logic itself.
questions.example: A notebook where cell 12 was deleted after defining adj_factor = 1.0025, but the variable is still live in the kernel's memory, will keep 'working' for the rest of the session while being completely unreproducible from a fresh Kernel Restart & Run All.
commonMistakes: Trusting a long-lived notebook's results without first confirming it survives a clean Restart & Run All
Treating the notebook's current working state as equivalent to a reproducible, on-disk record of the logic
Graduating the entire notebook (including exploratory plots and one-off diagnostics) rather than just the core logic
Not writing tests against the graduated module, losing the chance to formalize edge cases discovered informally
keyPoints: The hidden-state trap: a notebook's visible cell order and its actual execution history can silently diverge
Kernel Restart & Run All is the key diagnostic for whether a notebook's results are genuinely reproducible
Graduation means pulling only the core logic into a tested module, not the whole notebook
A thin, exploratory notebook should call the tested module afterward, rather than containing the real logic

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and explains the hidden-state trap as the urgent risk
Proposes Restart & Run All as the necessary first diagnostic step
Describes a concrete, sensible graduation process into a tested module
Clarity

questions.title: Evaluating Whether an Alternative Data Source Is Worth the Build
questions.prompt: A vendor is pitching a satellite-imagery dataset for estimating retail foot traffic. Design the evaluation process you'd run before committing engineering time to integrate it, and explain the specific compliance boundary that has to be checked regardless of how good the signal looks.
questions.modelAnswer: The evaluation process should be staged to spend the least effort first: start with the vendor's own claimed coverage and history length, since alternative data sources are frequently short-lived, before investing any integration effort. Next, a lightweight, cheap backtest on a small sample of the data to check whether the signal shows any discernible relationship to the target at all, before building a full production pipeline. Only once that passes should the team invest in full integration, through the standard data-layer interface, with the same point-in-time discipline every other data source requires. The compliance boundary that has to be checked regardless of how strong the signal looks is whether the data could constitute material non-public information (MNPI) -- that determination has to come from compliance and legal review, not from how good the backtest looks, since no amount of predictive power justifies trading on data that crosses that line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stage this specifically to avoid spending engineering time before knowing whether it's worth it. First, I'd just ask the vendor hard questions about history length and coverage, because alternative data sources are notoriously short-lived -- if this satellite program has only existed for two or three years, that alone might kill the idea before any code gets written. If the history checks out, I'd run the cheapest possible backtest on a small sample, just to see if there's any discernible relationship at all, before committing to a full integration with the same point-in-time discipline every other source has to meet. But regardless of how good any of that looks, there's one check that doesn't depend on the backtest at all: whether this data could be material non-public information. That's a compliance and legal determination, not something I'd ever let a strong backtest override.
questions.example: A satellite-imagery vendor with only 2 years of coverage history makes it impossible to test whether a foot-traffic signal held up through even one full market cycle, which alone is reason enough to defer integration regardless of the pitch's apparent strength.
commonMistakes: Committing to a full integration before checking the vendor's actual history length and coverage
Skipping a cheap, small-scale validation backtest before investing in production-grade engineering
Treating the MNPI compliance check as secondary to or overridable by a strong backtest result
Not applying the same point-in-time discipline to alternative data that other data sources are held to
keyPoints: Alternative data sources often have short history, which should be checked before any engineering investment
A cheap, small-scale validation backtest should precede full production integration
Full integration should still require point-in-time discipline, like any other data source
The MNPI compliance boundary must be checked independently of backtest performance, and can override it entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensibly staged evaluation process minimizing wasted effort
Correctly addresses point-in-time discipline for the new data source
Correctly identifies and explains the MNPI compliance boundary as independent of backtest results
Clarity

questions.title: Designing a Regime-Aware Model Routing Architecture
questions.prompt: You want a production system that clusters the current market into a regime (using something like a Gaussian Mixture Model) and routes to a different downstream model depending on which regime is detected. What architectural risk does this introduce that a single always-on model doesn't have, and how would you mitigate it?
questions.modelAnswer: A regime-routing architecture introduces a specific failure mode a single always-on model doesn't have: regime misclassification risk, where the clustering step is wrong about the current regime, routing the entire decision to a potentially completely wrong downstream model, compounding one error into a much larger one. This is especially dangerous near regime boundaries, where soft, probabilistic regime membership can be genuinely ambiguous, and a hard routing decision forces a confident choice exactly where the underlying signal is least confident. The mitigation: expose and log the regime-membership probabilities, using them to blend between downstream models rather than a brittle hard switch; build a regime-agnostic fallback model the system defers to whenever classification confidence falls below a threshold; and monitor regime-transition frequency against its historical base rate, since a sudden spike is itself a sign the clustering is becoming unstable.
questions.professionalAnswer: The specific risk this setup has that a single always-on model doesn't is that a wrong regime classification doesn't just degrade one model's output a little -- it can route the whole decision to a completely different, potentially wrong downstream model. That risk is worst right at regime boundaries, where soft membership probabilities are genuinely ambiguous, and forcing a hard routing decision there is asking the system to be confident exactly where the underlying signal isn't. My mitigation is two-pronged: first, I'd never throw away the soft membership probabilities in favor of just the hard cluster label -- I'd use them to blend between regime-specific models when the classification is ambiguous. Second, I'd build in a regime-agnostic fallback model the system leans toward whenever classification confidence drops below some threshold. I'd also track how often regime transitions happen in production against their historical base rate, since a sudden spike is itself a warning sign.
questions.example: A GaussianMixture emitting membership probabilities of [0.52, 0.48] between two regimes is effectively telling the system 'I don't actually know which regime this is' -- routing hard to either downstream model at that confidence level is forcing false certainty onto a genuinely ambiguous read.
commonMistakes: Using only the hard regime assignment and discarding the soft membership probabilities
Not building a fallback for low-confidence regime classifications, forcing a full commitment either way
Treating regime misclassification as a minor degradation rather than a compounding error through the whole downstream model
Not monitoring regime-transition frequency in production as a separate signal of clustering instability
keyPoints: Regime misclassification compounds into routing the entire decision to a potentially wrong downstream model
Regime boundaries are where soft membership probabilities are most ambiguous, and hard routing is riskiest there
Using soft membership probabilities to blend downstream models mitigates the hard-boundary risk
A regime-agnostic fallback model and monitoring of transition frequency add further protection

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the compounding misclassification risk unique to this architecture
Proposes using soft membership probabilities / blending rather than hard routing
Proposes a fallback mechanism and/or monitoring for regime instability
Clarity

questions.title: Building a Volatility Forecast Pipeline That Feeds a Live VaR Number
questions.prompt: Design the architecture of a pipeline that fits a GARCH-family model nightly and feeds a forward volatility forecast into a live Value-at-Risk number used by risk management the next trading day. What's the single most important validation step this pipeline needs that a pure research backtest wouldn't emphasize?
questions.modelAnswer: The pipeline needs three stages run nightly: refit the GARCH-family model on the latest return history (with a fallback to the previous day's parameters if the fit fails, rather than crashing or silently using garbage output), generate the forward variance forecast, and convert that into the VaR number. The single most important validation step a pure research backtest wouldn't naturally emphasize is live backtesting of the VaR forecast itself through violation/exception tracking: counting how often the actual realized loss exceeds the forecasted VaR threshold, and checking that exception rate against the theoretical rate implied by the VaR's confidence level. A research backtest validates the GARCH model's fit; it doesn't automatically validate whether the resulting VaR number has the right breach frequency in live production -- that operational validation (via something like a Kupiec test) has to run continuously, not just once at model deployment.
questions.professionalAnswer: The pipeline itself is three nightly stages: refit the GARCH model on fresh data, with a fallback to yesterday's parameters if the fit itself fails; generate the forward variance forecast; and convert that into the actual VaR figure. But the validation step I'd insist on, that a pure research backtest doesn't naturally push you toward, is ongoing exception tracking on the live VaR number itself -- counting how often the next day's actual loss actually breaches the VaR threshold, and checking that breach rate against what the VaR's own confidence level implies. A research backtest tends to validate the GARCH model's fit and its volatility forecast accuracy, which is necessary but not the same question as whether the VaR number it feeds is actually well-calibrated once it's running live. That's exactly the kind of ongoing operational check, something like a Kupiec test, that a risk committee would demand before trusting this for real limits.
questions.example: A 99% VaR model that's breached on 4% of trading days over a rolling year, rather than the expected ~1%, is failing a Kupiec-style exception test -- a signal the underlying volatility forecast is systematically too low, something a one-time research backtest of the GARCH fit alone would never have caught.
commonMistakes: Validating only the GARCH model's statistical fit, without separately validating the resulting VaR number's live breach rate
Not building a fallback for a nightly refit failure, risking a crashed pipeline or a silently bad forecast feeding risk limits
Treating model validation as a one-time deployment check rather than an ongoing operational monitor
Not using a formal statistical test (like Kupiec) to compare the observed exception rate against the theoretical rate
keyPoints: The nightly pipeline needs a safeguard (fallback) for a GARCH refit failure
A research backtest validates the volatility model's fit; it doesn't automatically validate the live VaR's breach rate
Ongoing exception/violation tracking on the live VaR number is the critical operational validation step
A formal test (e.g. Kupiec) comparing observed vs. theoretical breach rate is what a risk function would require

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a sensible nightly pipeline architecture with a refit-failure safeguard
Correctly distinguishes model-fit validation from live VaR exception validation
Proposes a concrete ongoing validation mechanism (exception tracking / Kupiec test)
Clarity

questions.title: Productionizing a Fama-French-Style Factor Pipeline
questions.prompt: You need to compute SMB and HML factor returns daily, in production, from a universe that gets its fundamental data from a vendor feed with a multi-week reporting lag. What's the architectural decision that determines whether this pipeline is point-in-time correct, and what happens if you get it wrong?
questions.modelAnswer: The architectural decision that determines point-in-time correctness is exactly how the pipeline handles the reporting lag between a fundamental data point's fiscal period and the date it actually became knowable: the pipeline must apply fundamental inputs only as of their real-world public availability date, not their fiscal period end date, and that availability date has to be tracked explicitly as its own field in the data layer rather than inferred as a fixed offset. If this is implemented wrong -- using the fiscal-period-end date as if it were the availability date -- the factor construction silently uses information nobody could have actually traded on: a book-value figure published six weeks after year-end gets incorporated into a sort as of the year-end date itself, introducing a small but systematic look-ahead bias throughout the entire history. Any research built on top of these factors inherits that bias without any obvious symptom -- the factor returns will look slightly better and smoother than real, tradeable factors would have been.
questions.professionalAnswer: The decision that actually determines correctness here is how the pipeline treats the gap between when a fundamental number describes (its fiscal period) and when it was actually knowable (its real public availability date) -- and that availability date needs to be its own explicit, tracked field in the data layer, not something inferred as a fixed lag. Get this wrong by using the fiscal period-end date as a stand-in for availability, and the pipeline is quietly using information nobody could have actually traded on at that date -- a book value only published six weeks after year-end gets baked into a sort as of the year-end itself, which means the daily SMB and HML series carry a small, systematic look-ahead bias through the entire history. What makes this dangerous is that the consequence doesn't show up as an obvious bug -- it shows up as factor returns that look slightly too good and slightly too smooth.
questions.example: A fundamental field recorded with fiscal_period_end=2024-03-31 but actual_availability_date=2024-05-10 should only be eligible for a sort computed on or after May 10 -- using it in an April sort is six weeks of silent look-ahead bias, repeated every quarter, for every name in the universe.
commonMistakes: Using a fundamental data point's fiscal period end date as if it were its real public availability date
Assuming a single fixed reporting lag applies uniformly across companies and filing types
Not tracking availability date as its own explicit field in the data layer
Not recognizing that this bias silently propagates into every downstream model or regression that uses the factors
keyPoints: Point-in-time correctness depends on using a fundamental's real availability date, not its fiscal period end date
Real reporting lags vary by company and filing type and should be tracked explicitly, not assumed as a fixed offset
Getting this wrong introduces a systematic, hard-to-detect look-ahead bias into the daily factor series
The bias silently propagates into any downstream model or regression built on top of the mis-specified factors

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies availability-date tracking as the key architectural decision
Correctly explains the look-ahead bias consequence of getting it wrong
Explains how the bias propagates to downstream research without an obvious symptom
Clarity

questions.title: Turning a Vague Idea Into a Falsifiable Research Question
questions.prompt: A portfolio manager tells you 'I think sectors overreact and then bounce back -- go look into that.' Walk through exactly how you'd turn that into a research question and hypothesis precise enough that the data could actually prove it wrong.
questions.modelAnswer: A vague hunch like 'sectors overreact and bounce back' isn't falsifiable as stated -- there's no specific prediction it makes that data could contradict, since 'overreact' and 'bounce back' have no defined timeframe, magnitude, or universe attached. Turning it into a real research question means pinning down every one of those: what counts as the universe, what counts as 'overreact' (a specific lookback window and threshold), what counts as 'bounce back' (a specific forward window and statistical test), and whether the effect is constant or conditional on another state variable. The resulting hypothesis should generate a specific, falsifiable prediction: 'a sector's trailing 5-day return is negatively rank-correlated with its forward 5-day return, and that correlation is stronger when the VIX is elevated' is a claim the data can directly confirm or reject. I'd also state explicitly what result would count as disconfirming the hypothesis before running anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd tell the PM is that 'sectors overreact and bounce back' isn't something data can actually prove or disprove yet, because it doesn't pin down a timeframe, a magnitude, or even a universe. I'd settle on sector ETFs rather than individual stocks, specifically because individual stocks carry a lot of company-specific noise. I'd define 'overreact' as something concrete, like a trailing 5-day return, and 'bounce back' as a specific forward window and test, like a rank correlation. And I'd ask whether the PM's real intuition is that this always happens, or more in certain conditions -- if the latter, I'd build that into the hypothesis directly. Before I ever run the test, I'd also write down explicitly what result would mean the hypothesis is wrong.
questions.example: A falsifiable version of the PM's hunch: 'over 2007-2025, a sector ETF's trailing 5-day return is negatively rank-correlated with its forward 5-day return, and this effect is significantly stronger in the top VIX tercile than the bottom tercile' -- specific enough that a clean null result would genuinely kill the idea.
commonMistakes: Starting to build a model or run tests before translating the vague idea into a precise, falsifiable hypothesis
Not specifying the universe, timeframe, and magnitude thresholds the original idea left undefined
Leaving out what result would actually disconfirm the hypothesis, inviting post-hoc redefinition of success
Choosing a noisy universe (individual stocks) when a lower-noise one (sector ETFs) better fits the question
keyPoints: A vague idea isn't falsifiable until universe, timeframe, magnitude, and test are all specified precisely
The resulting hypothesis should generate a specific prediction the data could directly contradict
Whether the effect is constant or conditional on another variable should be stated explicitly upfront
What would count as disconfirming evidence should be written down before running any test

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies why the original idea isn't falsifiable as stated
Proposes concrete choices (universe, timeframe, test) that make it precise
Explicitly addresses pre-committing to what would disconfirm the hypothesis
Clarity
