questions.title: Choosing the Right Universe Before Writing Any Code
questions.prompt: You're deciding whether to test a mean-reversion hypothesis on individual stocks or on sector ETFs. Walk through the actual tradeoff you'd explain to a stakeholder who assumes 'more granular data is always better.'
questions.modelAnswer: The instinct that 'more granular is always better' is understandable but wrong here. An individual stock's short-term return is dominated by idiosyncratic noise -- earnings surprises, analyst calls, company-specific news -- that has nothing to do with a broad, systematic mean-reversion mechanism, so testing on individual stocks means fighting through a mountain of noise to find a much smaller systematic signal. Sector ETFs solve this specifically: each one already diversifies away single-company noise by construction, so what's left in a sector ETF's short-term return is much closer to a genuine sector-wide over- or under-reaction. There's a real cost: fewer independent cross-sectional units means less statistical power, and a sector-level signal may not translate directly into an individual-stock strategy. But for testing whether the underlying mechanism exists at all, sector ETFs are the right level.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the stakeholder through why more granular isn't automatically better for this specific question. An individual stock's short-term return is mostly noise that has nothing to do with any broad reversal mechanism -- earnings surprises, analyst actions, idiosyncratic news -- so testing a mean-reversion hypothesis on individual stocks means wading through a huge amount of company-specific noise to find a much smaller systematic effect underneath. Sector ETFs already diversify that idiosyncratic noise away just by being a basket of dozens of names, so what's left in a sector ETF's short-term move is much closer to whatever genuine sector-wide reaction the hypothesis is actually trying to capture. I'd be honest about the real cost too -- 11 sectors gives a lot less statistical breadth than hundreds of individual stocks, and confirming the effect at the sector level doesn't automatically mean it translates into a tradeable single-stock strategy.
questions.example: A sector ETF's 5-day return is a diversified average across dozens of underlying names, which is exactly why it's a cleaner lens for testing a systematic reversal mechanism than any single stock's 5-day return, which is dominated by that one company's own news.
commonMistakes: Assuming more granular data is unconditionally better, without considering idiosyncratic noise
Testing a systematic hypothesis on individual stocks without accounting for company-specific noise drowning out the signal
Not being honest about the real cost of a lower-granularity universe (reduced statistical breadth)
Conflating 'confirming the effect exists at the sector level' with 'having a tradeable individual-stock strategy'
keyPoints: Individual stock returns are dominated by idiosyncratic, company-specific noise
A diversified basket like a sector ETF already removes most of that noise by construction
Lower-noise granularity is the right choice for testing whether a systematic mechanism exists at all
This choice has a real cost: less statistical breadth, and no automatic translation to single-stock trading

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the idiosyncratic-noise problem with individual stocks
Correctly explains why a sector ETF universe isolates the systematic signal better
Honestly states the real cost/tradeoff of the lower-granularity choice
Clarity

questions.title: Defining Success Before You've Seen the Results
questions.prompt: Before running a single test, you're asked to write down what would count as 'success' for a research project. Why does this matter so much, and what's the specific discipline you'd follow when writing it?
questions.modelAnswer: Defining success criteria before looking at results is the discipline of preregistration, and it matters because it's a reliable defense against a very human failure mode: once you've already seen a result, it's almost impossible not to retroactively rationalize whatever number came out as 'basically what I expected,' or to quietly shift the goalposts. Writing success criteria down in advance removes that flexibility: the criteria either were or weren't met, and there's no room to redefine what counts as a good outcome after the fact. The specific discipline is to be concrete and falsifiable: not 'the strategy should perform well' but 'net Sharpe ratio, computed via purged walk-forward validation with realistic transaction costs, above 0.5' -- specific enough that there's exactly one honest answer, decided before anyone has seen a single result.
questions.professionalAnswer: This matters because of something I've seen happen to good researchers, not just sloppy ones: once you've already seen a result, it's genuinely hard not to rationalize it after the fact -- a Sharpe of 0.4 somehow becomes 'actually a solid number for this kind of strategy' in a way it probably wouldn't have been described before anyone saw it. Writing success criteria down in advance takes that flexibility away entirely. My discipline for writing it is to make it exactly as specific and falsifiable as a hypothesis has to be -- not 'the strategy should perform reasonably well,' but something like 'net Sharpe, computed through purged walk-forward validation with realistic costs, above 0.5' -- specific enough that there's only one honest answer to whether it was actually hit, decided before anyone has seen a single result come back.
questions.example: A project plan that states 'success means net Sharpe (purged walk-forward, realistic costs) above 0.5' before any backtest is run leaves no room to later describe a 0.3 result as 'actually pretty good given market conditions.'
commonMistakes: Deciding what counts as success only after seeing how the results turn out
Writing vague success criteria ('perform well') instead of specific, falsifiable thresholds
Allowing success criteria to be silently redefined once a disappointing result comes in
Not specifying exactly how a metric will be computed (validation scheme, cost assumptions) alongside its threshold
keyPoints: Success criteria defined after seeing results invite unconscious rationalization and goalpost-shifting
Preregistering criteria before running any test removes that flexibility entirely
Criteria should be as specific and falsifiable as a hypothesis, not vague aspirational language
The exact computation method (validation scheme, cost assumptions) should be specified alongside the threshold

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the rationalization/goalpost-shifting risk this discipline defends against
Proposes a specific, concrete example of well-written success criteria
Clarity and professionalism

questions.title: A Teammate Took a Shortcut Cleaning the Data
questions.prompt: You discover that a teammate's data-cleaning step forward-filled missing days across a multi-week gap, rather than flagging it, because 'it was faster and the results looked fine.' How do you raise this, and what do you actually propose as the fix?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd raise this directly but focused on the specific, concrete risk rather than the general judgment that a shortcut was taken: forward-filling across a short, one-session gap is a defensible, narrow fix for an ordinary data-vendor hiccup, but forward-filling across a multi-week gap manufactures weeks of artificial, zero-volatility, unchanged-price observations that never actually happened -- and any model trained on that stretch is learning from fabricated data. I'd frame the conversation around that specific mechanism rather than 'you cut a corner.' The concrete fix: cap forward-fill at one session, and for any gap longer than that, flag the affected dates explicitly rather than silently filling them, so downstream code and anyone reading results later can see exactly which stretches are gap-affected.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd bring this up specifically and non-judgmentally, focused on the actual mechanism rather than the fact that a shortcut was taken. Forward-filling one missing day from an ordinary vendor hiccup is a reasonable, narrow fix -- but forward-filling across a multi-week gap means fabricating weeks of flat, zero-volatility price observations that never happened, and any model trained across that stretch is quietly learning from data that isn't real. That's the part I'd want the teammate to see clearly, because it's genuinely easy to miss. The fix I'd propose is concrete: cap any forward-fill at one session, and for anything longer than that, explicitly flag the affected dates rather than silently filling them, so whoever uses this data downstream can see exactly where the gaps are.
questions.example: A three-week forward-filled gap in a volatility feature means that entire stretch reports zero realized volatility, which a downstream model could learn to associate, spuriously, with whatever the actual subsequent return happened to be during that fabricated flat period.
commonMistakes: Raising the issue as a judgment of the teammate's competence rather than the specific data-quality mechanism
Not distinguishing a short, defensible forward-fill from a long, data-fabricating one
Proposing only to remove the shortcut without proposing a concrete, workable replacement (flagging long gaps explicitly)
Letting the issue slide because 'the results looked fine,' without checking whether that's actually true
keyPoints: Forward-filling across a short gap is a defensible fix; forward-filling across a long gap fabricates data
A model trained on fabricated flat data is learning from something that never happened, distorting results invisibly
The conversation should focus on the specific mechanism and risk, not a judgment of the teammate
The concrete fix is capping forward-fill at one session and explicitly flagging longer gaps instead

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Handles the conversation constructively, focused on the mechanism rather than blame
Correctly explains why a long forward-fill fabricates data and distorts results
Proposes a specific, concrete fix (cap + explicit flagging)
Clarity

questions.title: Giving a Checkpoint Update When the Statistics Are Only Weakly Supportive
questions.prompt: Your hypothesis test came back statistically significant but small -- a correlation of -0.07 with a t-stat around -2.4. You have to give a go/no-go recommendation to a research-desk lead at the Phase 1 checkpoint. What do you actually say?
questions.modelAnswer: A statistically significant but small effect deserves a nuanced go/no-go, not a binary enthusiastic yes or a dismissive no: a correlation of -0.07 with a properly-corrected t-stat of -2.4 is real evidence against the null, but it's also a genuinely small effect size, and I'd state both facts plainly. My actual recommendation would be a conditional go: proceed into feature engineering and modeling, specifically because a small but statistically real effect is exactly the kind of signal that further conditioning can sometimes sharpen into something more tradeable -- but I'd pair that recommendation with an explicit, upfront statement of what the next checkpoint needs to show to keep going. I'd also flag honestly that with several related statistical cuts already run on the same dataset, a modest multiple-testing haircut on how much confidence to place in the exact t-stat is warranted.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd be straightforward with the research-desk lead about exactly what -0.07 with a t-stat of -2.4 does and doesn't mean: it's real evidence against the null, this isn't noise, but it's also a small effect, and I wouldn't want to oversell it. My actual recommendation is a conditional go, not an unconditional one -- I'd say we should move into feature engineering, because a small but statistically real effect is exactly the kind of thing that further conditioning can sometimes sharpen into something genuinely tradeable. But I'd pair that with a clear statement of what has to be true at the next checkpoint for us to keep going -- if the effect doesn't survive proper out-of-sample validation with real transaction costs, that's the point to stop. I'd also be upfront that we've already run several related cuts on this same dataset, so I'd apply a bit of a mental multiple-testing haircut.
questions.example: A go/no-go framed as 'proceed to Phase 2, with an explicit kill criterion: if the effect doesn't survive purged walk-forward out-of-sample testing with realistic costs, or shows no meaningful VIX-regime conditioning, we stop there' gives the desk lead a clear decision without overselling a modest effect.
commonMistakes: Giving a binary, overly enthusiastic 'yes, it's significant, let's go' without acknowledging the effect is small
Giving a dismissive 'it's too small to matter' without acknowledging it's genuinely statistically significant
Not stating upfront what the next checkpoint needs to show to justify continuing
Failing to disclose that multiple related statistical cuts were already run on the same dataset
keyPoints: A small but statistically significant effect deserves a conditional, not binary, go/no-go recommendation
The recommendation should state plainly that the effect is both real and small, not oversell either fact
An explicit kill criterion for the next checkpoint should be stated upfront, before further work proceeds
Multiple related statistical tests on the same data warrant disclosing a mental multiple-testing caveat

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Gives an honest, nuanced characterization of the statistical result (real but small)
Proposes a specific, conditional go/no-go recommendation with clear stopping criteria
Discloses the multiple-testing caveat appropriately
Clarity and professionalism

questions.title: Writing a Capstone Bullet That Survives a Technical Follow-Up
questions.prompt: You're writing your resume bullet for a research capstone project. A recruiter told you quant resumes get read by people who 'built and broke strategies like yours for a living.' Write the bullet you'd actually use, and explain what makes it survive a skeptical follow-up question rather than collapse under one.
questions.modelAnswer: A bullet that survives a technical follow-up has to be specific enough that the interviewer's natural next question is already partially answered: 'Researched and validated a cross-sectional mean-reversion signal across 11 sector ETFs (2007-2025), using purged walk-forward cross-validation; achieved net Sharpe 0.42 after realistic transaction costs, versus 0.76 gross' is a bullet that already answers 'how did you validate it' and 'did you account for costs' before the interviewer has to ask. A bullet like 'Built a profitable trading strategy with Sharpe 1.8' collapses immediately under a single follow-up, because it was written to sound impressive rather than to survive scrutiny. The discipline behind writing a bullet that holds up is the same discipline the research itself should have followed: lead with the honest, net number and the real validation method.
questions.professionalAnswer: The bullet I'd actually write is something like: 'Researched and validated a cross-sectional mean-reversion signal across 11 sector ETFs (2007-2025) using purged walk-forward cross-validation; net Sharpe 0.42 after realistic transaction costs, versus 0.76 gross.' What makes that survive a follow-up is that it already answers the two questions a skeptical interviewer is going to ask anyway -- how was this validated, and is that number gross or net. Compare that to something like 'Built a profitable strategy with Sharpe 1.8,' which falls apart the instant someone asks 'gross or net, and how was it validated,' because it was clearly written to sound impressive rather than to hold up under scrutiny. Writing a bullet that survives that is really just applying the same honesty the research itself should have had in the first place.
questions.example: 'Researched and validated a cross-sectional mean-reversion signal across 11 sector ETFs (2007-2025) using purged walk-forward cross-validation; net Sharpe 0.42 after realistic transaction costs, versus 0.76 gross' pre-answers the two most likely follow-up questions before they're asked.

Omitting the validation methodology, leaving an obvious opening for 'how did you test this'
Writing for maximum impressiveness rather than for surviving a skeptical technical follow-up
Not recognizing that quant interviewers specifically probe for exactly the gaps an oversold bullet leaves open

questions.title: Thinking Out Loud Through a Classic Probability Brainteaser
questions.prompt: An interviewer asks: 'You flip a fair coin repeatedly. What's the expected number of flips until you see two heads in a row?' Walk through exactly how you'd structure your answer out loud, not just the final number.
questions.modelAnswer: The structure matters as much as the answer, since interviewers are scoring the reasoning process, not just whether the final number happens to be right. I'd start by narrating the setup explicitly: define states by the most recent flip -- state S0 (start, or last flip was tails) and state S1 (last flip was heads) -- and let E0, E1 be the expected additional flips from each state. From S0: E0 = 1 + 0.5*E1 + 0.5*E0. From S1: E1 = 1 + 0.5*0 + 0.5*E0. Solving out loud: the first equation rearranges to E0 = 2 + E1; substituting gives E0 = 3 + 0.5*E0, so E0 = 6. I'd finish with a sanity check -- does 6 feel right given that getting one head takes 2 flips on average, and extending that into a pair without breaking should take a bit longer -- rather than just stating the number and stopping.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd narrate every step out loud rather than silently working it out and announcing a number, because the interviewer is scoring how I think, not just whether I land on 6. I'd start by setting up states based on the most recent flip -- S0 if the last flip wasn't a head, S1 if it was -- and define E0 and E1 as the expected number of additional flips from each state. From S0, the next flip either moves me to S1 or keeps me at S0, so E0 equals 1 plus half of E1 plus half of E0. From S1, the next flip either finishes the job or sends me back to S0, so E1 equals 1 plus half of zero plus half of E0. I'd work through the algebra out loud -- E0 equals 2 plus E1, substituting gives E0 equals 3 plus half of E0, so E0 equals 6 -- and I'd close with a quick sanity check against intuition rather than just stopping at the number.
questions.example: A 200,000-trial simulation of this exact process confirms the sample mean lands around 5.99, matching the exact analytical answer of 6 -- a good habit to mention even without actually running it, as a way of showing how you'd verify your own answer.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to a memorized final answer without narrating the state-based reasoning
Going silent while working through the algebra instead of talking through each step
Not performing a final sanity check on whether the resulting number is intuitively plausible
Treating silence as safer than a partial, honest attempt when genuinely stuck mid-derivation
keyPoints: Interviewers score the structured reasoning process, not just the final number
Defining explicit states based on the most recent outcome is the standard technique for this problem family
Working the resulting system of equations out loud, step by step, demonstrates process, not just conclusion
A closing sanity check against intuition is itself part of a strong answer
